name: Vilayil Veedu (Karamana) — Onavillu makers
tagline: Hereditary carpenters of Karamana who craft the sacred Onavillu for temple ritual
summary: A hereditary carpentry family in Karamana, Thiruvananthapuram, the Vilayil Veedu make the colourful, painted Onavillu (ceremonial bows) offered at Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple each Onam.
description: The Vilayil Veedu family of Melarannoor, Karamana, practices a hereditary carpentry tradition that produces the Onavillu — colourful, hand‑painted ceremonial bows offered at Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple during Onam. The right to make the temple Onavillu is traditionally vested in this family.

Onavillu are wooden, flat bows painted in the panchavarna (five colours) and decorated with tassels; panels depict Vishnu’s avatars and other sacred imagery. The craft combines careful carpentry, surface preparation and painting in a compact family workshop.

The family works seasonally but also makes smaller devotional Onavillu for devotees and for sale. Visitors who see or photograph the work should request permission and respect the ritual purpose of the objects.

This living tradition appears in state tourism and news coverage and continues to supply the temple ritual each Onam; the craft receives occasional coverage in local press and responsible‑tourism listings.
highlights: Hereditary carpentry family (Vilayil Veedu) based at Melarannoor, Karamana.
They make the Onavillu offered at Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple on Thiruvonam.
Onavillu use panchavarna painting and are made from traditional woods.
Family produces both full‑size ceremonial bows and smaller devotional models.
Craft blends joinery, surface gesso/priming and fine hand‑painting.

sections.heading: Background
body: Onavillu are ceremonial bows offered during Onam as part of the rituals at Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram. The Vilayil Veedu family of Karamana (also reported as Vaniyam‑moola Vilayil) holds the traditional right to make these bows and supplies the temple and devotees.

Local and tourism sources describe the family as the sole traditional makers who prepare the set of bows presented on Thiruvonam; the practice appears in Kerala Tourism material and multiple local news features.

sections.heading: Materials and technique
body: Onavillu are flat, plank‑like bows (often 3.5–4.5 ft long in traditional descriptions) cut from woods such as kadambu or mahogany, finished smooth and primed for painting. Artisans apply the panchavarna (five colours: white, green, red, yellow and black) to depict Vishnu’s avatars and sacred motifs, and add red tassels as decoration.

Work is family‑based and combines woodworking (shaping, sanding, finishing) with a distinct regional painting style. The making is both craft and ritual — historically the bows are first offered at the family’s own shrine before temple dedication.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Visitors can observe panel preparation, painting and finishing when the family is working (particularly in the leadup to Onam). The family also makes smaller Onavillu that devotees purchase as keepsakes or offerings. Ask permission before photographing or filming, and avoid disrupting work.

Because the work is tied to temple ritual and seasonality, contact or visit with local tourism outlets or the family (confirm before you travel) to check whether makers are available outside the Onam period.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Karamana is a suburb of Thiruvananthapuram city; plan visits from the city and combine with a visit to the Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple precincts. Makers are busiest during Chingam (Onam season), so expect workshops to be active then and small Onavillu to be in stock.

Respect ritual norms: Onavillu are sacred objects offered in temple worship. If you want to buy a devotional or decorative Onavillu, buy directly from the family or authorised sellers and confirm availability and price before you go.

latest.text: A March–April 2026 publication references Binkumar Achary’s family and Vilayil Veedu among contemporary Onavillu practitioners, confirming ongoing practice into 2026.
Kerala electoral/administrative records in January 2026 list Vilayil Veedu (Melarannoor, Karamana), corroborating the family's local presence and address details on public records.
Local press reports in July 2024 state the Karamana Melarannoor Vilayil Veedu family will continue to make and dedicate Onavillu at the temple, underlining the ritual continuity.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Chingam (Onam season, August–September); busiest and most active around Thiruvonam day.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Karamana is in Thiruvananthapuram city. Reach by road from the city; Thiruvananthapuram has the nearest major railway station and airport. Contact the family or local tourism desk to confirm availability before you visit.
etiquette: Confirm availability before you travel — the family is busiest around Onam and may work seasonally.
Ask permission before photographing or filming the workshop and ritual objects.
Prefer buying small devotional Onavillu directly from the makers or authorised sellers; confirm price and delivery terms.
Respect the sacred purpose of Onavillu — treat finished pieces as devotional objects, not just souvenirs.
